title: Given a list of words sorted according to an unknown alphabet, derive a valid ordering of the characters in that alphabet. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Alien Dictionary (Derive Character Order from a Sorted Word List)

s1_definition.profdef: The Alien Dictionary is a graph-construction application of the Topological Sort pattern. From each adjacent pair of sorted words we find the first differing character, which gives a directed edge showing that one character precedes another. We then topologically sort the characters with Kahn's algorithm to produce a valid alphabet, detecting contradictions as cycles. This runs in linear time in the total input size.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India receives a list of product tier codes already sorted by an internal ranking whose rule is unknown, and it wants to recover the ranking of the individual tier symbols. The Alien Dictionary derives that symbol order from the sorted list.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each adjacent word pair's first difference gives one ordering edge, then topologically sort the characters.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Alien Dictionary is a graph-construction application of the Topological Sort pattern. From each adjacent pair of sorted words we find the first differing character, which gives a directed edge showing that one character precedes another. We then topologically sort the characters with Kahn's algorithm to produce a valid alphabet, detecting contradictions as cycles. This runs in linear time in the total input size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India receives a list of product tier codes already sorted by an internal ranking whose rule is unknown, and it wants to recover the ranking of the individual tier symbols. The Alien Dictionary derives that symbol order from the sorted list.

**One line to remember:** Each adjacent word pair's first difference gives one ordering edge, then topologically sort the characters.

sections.s2_technical:
We first collect every distinct character so each becomes a node. Then for each adjacent pair of words we compare them character by character until we find the first position where they differ: that tells us the character in the earlier word comes before the character in the later word, so we add a directed edge and increment the in-degree of the later character. An important edge case is that if the earlier word is a prefix of the later word everything is fine, but if the later word is a strict prefix of the earlier word the input is invalid.

After building the graph we run Kahn's algorithm over the characters, enqueuing zero in-degree characters and appending them as we remove them, relaxing edges along the way. The core edge extraction is `for the first index where a.charAt(k) != b.charAt(k): adj.get(a.charAt(k)).add(b.charAt(k)); indeg.merge(b.charAt(k), 1, Integer::sum); break;`. If the final order omits any character a cycle made the ordering contradictory. A concrete check: words that sort as the list implies B before A yields an alphabet with B before A. Senior nuance: this is linear in the total number of characters across all words, the prefix check prevents an invalid dictionary from slipping through, and only the first differing character gives information.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives product tier codes sorted by an internal ranking whose ordering rule over the individual symbols is unknown, and it needs to recover the rank order of the symbols so it can apply the same ranking elsewhere. Guessing the order is unreliable. This is exactly how the Alien Dictionary works: it extracts ordering edges from adjacent sorted codes and topologically sorts the symbols with the Topological Sort pattern.

The code defines a `TierOrderService` exposing `deriveSymbolOrder(sortedCodes)` returning a string of symbols in valid order, empty on contradiction. A `Demo` runs it over a small sorted code list and logs the derived order.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the sorted code list ba, bc, ac, cab. We want the order of the symbols a, b, c.

Step 1 — We collect the distinct symbols a, b, and c as nodes, each starting with in-degree zero.

Step 2 — Comparing ba and bc, the first difference is at position one where a comes before c, so we add an edge from a to c and raise c's in-degree to one.

Step 3 — Comparing bc and ac, the first difference is at position zero where b comes before a, so we add an edge from b to a and raise a's in-degree to one.

Step 4 — Comparing ac and cab, the first difference is at position zero where a comes before c, an edge we already have, so c's in-degree stays consistent. Now b has in-degree zero, a has in-degree one, and c has in-degree one.

Step 5 — Kahn's algorithm starts with b, then a once its in-degree drops to zero, then c, giving the order b, a, c. All three symbols appear, so there is no contradiction. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:51:44 PM com.bank.tierorder.service.TierOrderService deriveSymbolOrder
INFO: Derived symbol order = bac
Oct 27, 2026 9:51:44 PM com.bank.tierorder.TierOrderApplication main
INFO: Recovered tier symbol order: bac
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: sorted codes = [ba, bc, ac, cab]
    │
    ▼
  first-difference edges:
    │ ba vs bc → a→c  (indeg c=1)
    │ bc vs ac → b→a  (indeg a=1)
    │ ac vs cab → a→c (already present)
    ▼
  Kahn: start b (indeg 0) → a (indeg 0) → c
    ▼
  Output: symbol order = "bac"  (all symbols placed, no cycle)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Alien Dictionary is a graph-construction application of the Topological Sort pattern, where the real work is turning sorted words into ordering edges before I sort anything. I first register every distinct character as a node, then I walk through each adjacent pair of words and compare them character by character until the first position where they differ. That first difference is the only informative one, and it tells me the character from the earlier word precedes the character from the later word, so I add a directed edge and raise the in-degree of the later character.

I watch for the invalid case where the later word is a strict prefix of the earlier word, because a correctly sorted dictionary can never do that. Once the graph is built I run Kahn's algorithm over the characters, enqueuing zero in-degree characters and appending them as I remove them. If the final order omits any character, a cycle made the ordering contradictory and I return empty. The whole thing is linear in the total number of characters across the words.

At the National Bank of India I used this to recover the rank order of product tier symbols from a list of tier codes that were sorted by an internal ranking whose rule over the symbols was unknown. I extracted the ordering edges from adjacent codes and topologically sorted the symbols. Explaining that only the first differing character gives an edge, that a later-word-prefix case is invalid, and that a cycle means contradiction is what shows an interviewer I understand this construction-plus-sort use of the Topological Sort pattern.
